articles.title: A New Blockbuster Trade Idea To Save Devin Booker
articles.summary: The Phoenix Suns won't hear any trade talk around superstar Devin Booker.
articles.body:
The Phoenix Suns won't hear any trade talk around superstar Devin Booker.

That doesn't mean the speculation is going away.

The 30-year-old five-time All-Star is a win-now contributor on a club lacking both win-now support and the longterm assets needed to acquire it. They don't have a co-star to pair with Booker. Or a starting-caliber point guard. Or nearly enough defensive stoppers.

Booker badly needs a scenery change (even if he won't admit it ). The Suns need to pave a path toward a brighter future (even if they'll deny interest). And the championship picture could change the second those realizations are made.

Let's get into the how and why of such a landscape-shifting Booker blockbuster.

Toronto Raptors receive: Devin Booker, Luke Kennard (trade eligible Dec. 15)

Phoenix Suns receive: RJ Barrett, Immanuel Quickley, 2029 first-round pick, 2030 first-round pick swap

After paying a premium to bring Kawhi Leonard back north of the border this offseason, the Raptors could effectively double down with this deal for Booker.

The Leonard-Scottie Barnes combo can be special, but it isn't the most reliable by production or availability. Booker could stabilize both sides, plus provide the potent scoring threat needed to better space the floor.

Defenses currently content with forcing RJ Barrett or Immanuel Quickley to beat them would want no part of placing the same wager with Booker, who has basically been a 26-point, six-assist machine for a decade now. Having him, Leonard and Barnes in the same offense would present a true pick-your-poison puzzle for opponents.

It's an aggressive move to ship out a starting backcourt, obviously, but Toronto already veered into aggressive mode with that Leonard deal. And this could be the time to floor the pedal with the Philadelphia 76ers struggling to connect their dots on offense, and the Boston Celtics and Detroit Pistons facing the same one-star concern. (Not to mention the letdown showings from the New York Knicks and Cleveland Cavaliers.)

Plus, Booker could be a big upgrade over Barrett. Booker's heavy offensive burden has hurt his efficiency, but he's had elite shooting seasons when he's had help around him. The Raptors could lean on energizer Jamal Shead to fill Quickley's vacated spot and let Kennard run wild as an off-ball sharpshooter.

Toronto feels close to a contending-level breakthrough. Without that belief, it never would've brought Leonard back. A second daring deal could be key in making that dream a reality.

If the Suns ever moved on from Booker, their recent history suggests they wouldn't be interested in bottoming out. And after the league's lottery reforms, tanking is sort of off the table for now anyway.

Should Phoenix want to remain semi-competitive, it could. Quickley is a legitimate starting point guard, which the Suns are currently (and notably) without. Barrett is another solid starter and capable scorer, averaging 20-plus points for the fourth time in the last six seasons.

The Suns need better scoring depth, and this incoming combo could help provide it. If this meant repurposing Jalen Green as a quick-strike sixth man (which might be his ideal NBA calling), this offense could come out of this in better shape, or at least no worse.

That would be a sizable victory, since the draft capital is the real prize for Phoenix. The Suns could try holding out for more, but a future first-round pick and a future first-round pick swap (both unprotected) would be a hefty haul for a 30-year-old who could be more really good than great—while being paid as a no-doubt elite ( roughly $250 million between now and 2029-30).

The swap would still carry a short-term sting for the fanbase, especially after the organization's many public pushbacks about the mere notion of a Booker trade. They'd get over it. As much as they might like Booker, they can't feel great about their present (sub-.500 with a bottom-third net rating ) and might feel worse about their future (shortage of draft picks and prospects).

This would give Phoenix the chance to take a fairly large step forward in the future without having to witness a sizable stepback right now. Under their circumstances, that might qualify as a win-win.

articles.title: New 2027 NBA Mock Draft with Full 2-Round Predictions, Pro Comps
articles.summary: First impressions are out on this year's NBA draft class, and the general feeling seems positive.
articles.body:
First impressions are out on this year's NBA draft class, and the general feeling seems positive.

Even if a lack of obvious star power is evident, most of the top prospects have looked good early, and we've already started to see breakouts that should help strengthen the class' depth.

The popular preseason No. 1, Tyran Stokes, hasn't disappointed at Kansas. It's the next tier that's up in the air and accessible for a wide variety of prospects to break into.

The next few weeks represent key evaluation periods, particularly with the Players Era tournaments taking place in Las Vegas. Almost all of the NBA scouting community will be at one of the two, as the majority of top prospects will be participating.

1. New Orleans Pelicans (via Bucks): Tyran Stokes (Kansas)

Position: SF/PF | Size: 6'8", 230 lbs | Age: 18

After a 27-point, seven assist preseason game against Duke, Tyran Stokes passed his first big regular season test against Kentucky. With scouting eyes focused on his shooting stroke, decision-making and attitude, he drilled four threes, looked patient in the half court, aggressive in transition and poised throughout the game.

While confidence from scouts isn't as high in Stokes as it's been for previous projected No. 1 overall picks, he's done nothing so far to scare anyone off while also showcasing a very enticing package of power, playmaking and diverse shotmaking.

In a draft cycle lacking obvious star-level talent, rebuilding teams are counting on Stokes.

2. Sacramento Kings: Caleb Holt (Arizona)

Position: SG | Size: 6'5", 215 lbs | Age: 18

Caleb Holt's athleticism, motor and versatility create a high-floor label, which teams may value more in a draft lacking obvious stars. But games like the one he put together against Auburn, when he scored 24 points and delivered flashes of self-creation and confident shotmaking, suggest there's more offensive upside he can unlock.

Arizona will be using him in a variety of ways from different spots. Though Holt may not have one specialty skill, he'll find ways to produce with physical drives, spot-up threes, off-ball finishing, offensive rebounding, secondary playmaking and disruptive defense.

3. Chicago Bulls: Quentin Coleman (Illinois)

Position: PG/SG | Size: 6'4", 180 lbs | Age: 18

Pro comparison: Nickeil Alexander-Walker

Quentin Coleman has become one of the buzziest names in the draft discussion, particularly after he nearly carried Illinois back against Texas Tech despite vomiting earlier in the half. Questions about his 180-pound frame won't disappear, but they aren't setting off alarms thanks to his shooting range, athletic and IQ plays.

The hype keeps building around his game, which includes a well-rounded mix of shotmaking, creativity, explosive rim plays and a high motor.

His stock will rise if he can continue to demonstrate lead-guard skills as a ball-handler and playmaker, rather than project as a 180-pound combo guard who leans toward the 2.

Latest 2027 Men's NCAA Tournament Bracket Projections

4. Houston Rockets (via Nets): Bruce Branch III (BYU)

Bruce Branch III is off to an efficient start that's shined light on his advantageous tools and shotmaking.

His scoring potential has looked convincing early, with Branch using his body effectively on drives, showing signs of self-creation and converting enough jumpers through BYU's first batch of games.

He's also delivered some assists that really highlight encouraging passing IQ, which should help create some extra cushion if Branch's shooting consistency fluctuates.

5. Washington Wizards: Jordan Smith Jr. (Arkansas)

Position: PG/SG | Size: 6'2", 205 lbs | Age: 19

Jordan Smith Jr. has drawn mixed early reviews around his outstanding physicality/athleticism and questionable perimeter scoring.

Unsurprisingly, he's been at his best tapping into his strength, quickness and burst for transition scoring and applying defensive pressure. He's been less convincing in the half court, where he's looked reluctant to shoot threes and too comfortable taking step-back twos.

Outside shooting limitations and 6'2" size are the likely drawbacks that could make scouts hesitate to project Smith in the top three—especially if he's not able to show the type of playmaking scouts want from a lead guard.

Still, there's a high floor attached to Smith's outlook, given how easy it is to picture his explosion and intensity translating to rim pressure, paint buckets and disruptive defense. And though not a shooter, he's still flashed enough shotmaking over the years for scouts to feel confident he'll maintain the ability to hit mid-range pull-ups and rhythm threes.

There may be debate about Smith Jr.'s NBA ceiling, but he'll remain popular in a class without obvious stars.

6. Memphis Grizzlies (via Jazz): Stefan Joksimovic (Baskonia)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'7" | Age: 18 | Slovenia

Many NBA teams sent scouts to Europe during early November to get their first live looks at Stefan Joksimovic. They picked a good time to visit—the 18-year-old saw increased playing time and subsequent scoring chances to show off his advantageous mix of size, ball-handling, open-floor fluidity and shotmaking potential.

While Joksimovic has struggled with his jump shot, there is enough tape/evidence for scouts to remain optimistic. The bigger questions NBA teams will have revolve around his ability to create against and defend quicker, more athletic wings.

He may develop skeptics who'll hesitate to rank him in the same tier as the top NCAA prospects, but given his age, production and archetype—a big playmaker with on and off-ball skills and tools—Joksimovic figures to continue looking like an enticing bet in this particular draft.

7. Atlanta Hawks (via Pelicans): Alijah Arenas (USC)

Position: SG | Size: 6'6", 199 lbs | Age: 19

Alijah Arenas' start is what scouts have asked for—efficient scoring fueled by advanced moves and smarter shot selection within USC's offense.

There isn't a more convincing shot-creator in the class, thanks to Arenas' tight handles, improvisation and advantageous height and release point. So far, the shots are falling from every level.

While scouts seem willing to forgive last year's 34.1 percent shooting from the field, which came after a late start to the season following a meniscus tear , Arenas has to be able to maintain a certain level of efficiency throughout the year.

The microwave-scoring, non-playmaker archetype has lost value in the NBA, and any signs of ball-stopping or icing out teammates have the potential to quickly turn scouts back off.

8. Charlotte Hornets: Patrick Ngongba II (Duke)

Position: C | Size: 6'11", 250 lbs | Age: 20

Patrick Ngongba II has made strong first impressions, looking healthy, toned and more involved offensively.

The draw to the 6'11", 250-pound center will always revolve around his ability to operate as a playmaking hub and defensive anchor. But with more touches this year, he's shown to be a threatening low-post scorer and foul-drawer with his strength and footwork.

His three-point attempt rate is also up, which could be a needle-mover if he's able to demonstrate some convincing improvement with his shooting range.

Otherwise, staying healthy, particularly his feet and legs, will be key to easing concerns about Ngongba.

9. Oklahoma City Thunder (via Clippers): Braylon Mullins (Connecticut)

Position: SG | Size: 6'6", 198 lbs | Age: 20

A regular name in 2026 first-round conversations, Braylon Mullins should be right back in the mix based on his productive start with more looks.

There's no mystery about how he'll be used at the next level. Mullins will fit easily with how well he's able to play off the ball and use movement to earn scoring chances and threes. And though not a realistic creator option, he's been effective early in ball-screen situations using pacing, floater touch and a potent pull-up game.

10. Houston Rockets (via Suns): Ivan Kharchenkov (Arizona)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'7", 220 lbs | Age: 19 | Russia/Germany

Ivan Kharchenkov's versatility and defensive toughness continue to shine in a bigger role.

Even with low three-point volume, he's a likable prospect as a 6'7", 220-pound wing who can attack, handle and pass, finish plays, defend and make mid-range shots.

Kharchenkov could profile as a plug-and-play role player for NBA teams, especially if he's able to show improved shooting range.

11. Indiana Pacers: Davis Fogle (Gonzaga)

Position: SF | Size: 6'7", 200 lbs | Age: 20

Gonzaga has trusted Davis Fogle in a lead role, and he's embraced it, looking comfortable getting to spots and confident rising into finishes and pull-ups.

He's even used his usage to become a playmaker, another sign of his expanding creativity off the dribble.

Between Fogle's positional size, athleticism around the rim, ball-handling development, three-level shotmaking skills and passing, he's starting to look like one of the class' more well-rounded wing prospects.

12. Los Angeles Clippers (via Raptors): Amari Allen (Alabama)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'6", 205 lbs | Age: 20

Offense is running through Amari Allen, who's having success attacking downhill and stepping into pull-ups. But his assist rate has popped most early, with Allen making skilled, live-dribble passes, quick connective passes and smart transition reads.

At the next level, he'll be valued more for versatility than straight-up scoring. He profiles more as a Swiss Army knife ball-handler and wing than a reliable creator.

13. Charlotte Hornets (via Mavericks): Thomas Haugh (Florida)

Position: SF/PF | Size: 6'9", 215 lbs | Age: 23

Late lottery teams will look past age if they see the same Thomas Haugh as last year with more consistent shooting.

Regardless of what Haugh's ceiling looks like, teams should remain interested in a 6'9" three-point threat and explosive finisher who'll make connective, high-IQ plays and bring regular intensity. Teams will value his easy fit and archetype over the potential upside.

Age will be a talking point, since he'll turn 24 right after the 2027 draft. Still, we just saw the Golden State Warriors take Yaxel Lendeborg No. 11 after Michigan's title, and the translatability of Haugh's game could earn similar treatment.

14. Golden State Warriors: Obinna Ekezie Jr. (Louisville)

Position: C | Size: 7'2", 240 lbs | Age: 18 | Nigeria

With Obinna Ekezie Jr. standing 7'2" with a 7'5" wingspan, any signs of outlier shooting or movement skills will generate NBA buzz.

His four three-pointers and five blocks against Kansas in the preseason initially turned heads. More lines like that would make Ekezie one of the class' most coveted bigs.

Between the Players Era field in Las Vegas and nonconference games against Texas, Michigan and Kentucky, Ekezie will have plenty of early chances to sell his NBA tools and offensive developmental progress.

15. Orlando Magic: Colben Landrew (Connecticut)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'6", 236 lbs | Age: 18

With Nik Khamenia out, Colben Landrew looks set for a sizable role and a green light to launch threes, attack defenders and run in transition.

He instantly passes the eye test with a 236-pound frame and rhythm behind his shooting stroke. There's also convincing high school tape of Landrew using his handle, strength and shotmaking versatility to score from three levels off drives and self-created jumpers.

He's set up to succeed with a point guard like Silas Demary Jr., teammates on the wing who'll draw top defenders and a coach willing to use freshmen.

16. Oklahoma City Thunder (via Nuggets): Abdou Toure (Arkansas)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'5", 200 lbs | Age: 18 | Guinea/USA

Abdou Toure's identity for Arkansas will revolve around his athleticism and motor for play-finishing and defense.

Signs of improving ball-handling and shotmaking should convince scouts to get in early on Toure.

It's easy to see Toure thriving in a two-way energizer role, but for a 6'5" guard, he'll become more of a return-to-school candidate if his creation and three-point shooting appear too limited.

17. Utah Jazz (via Cavaliers): Motiejus Krivas (Arizona)

Position: C | Size: 7'2", 260 lbs | Age: 21 | Lithuania

Motiejus Krivas likely would have gone in the first round in 2026, but he's now in position to become college basketball's most impactful big and a 2027 lottery pick.

NBA teams continue to value massive defensive centers like Donovan Clingan, Zach Edey and Aday Mara. Krivas is next in line at 7'2", 260 pounds, a frame he uses to shrink the rim he's protecting.

Though he won't be for everyone, teams looking for an immediate paint presence figure to view him as a long-term anchor.

18. Brooklyn Nets (via Knicks): Na'jai Hines (Connecticut)

Position: C | Size: 6'11", 278 lbs | Age: 19

On a per-minute basis, no player in the country combined better shot-blocking and offensive rebounding rates than Na'jai Hines last season.

Despite lacking any real creation or scoring skills beyond finishing and post-ups, his paint presence and defense are strong enough for scouts to look past the limited offensive versatility. He appeared to be in good shape and lighter on his feet during Connecticut's preseason, which could lead to more transition and easy baskets.

19. Charlotte Hornets (via Heat): Miikka Muurinen (Arkansas)

Position: PF/C | Size: 7'0", 215 lbs | Age: 19 | Finland

Miikka Muurinen will generate highlights and excitement with explosive finishing and shotmaking for a 7-footer. He's also likely to stir up conversation about his maturity and decision-making, which have been questioned by both former coaches overseas and scouts.

He hasn't shot well early, and an inefficient start has highlighted the fact that he's reliant on spot-up shooting and tools/athleticism for finishing.

Muurinen clearly possesses NBA physical talent and a coveted skill set for the position. Picking the right spots to attack offensively and avoiding emotional decision-making will be his lottery ticket.

20. San Antonio Spurs (via Hawks): JJ Andrews (Arkansas)

Position: SF | Size: 6'6", 225 lbs | Age: 18

JJ Andrews will give Arkansas physical two-point scoring, capable three-point shooting and strong tools for defending various archetypes.

Scouts will admire his 225-pound frame and developing perimeter skill, a combination that creates inside-out versatility and the ability to play/guard both forward positions.

Andrews should be an efficient, impactful player in a supporting role, and his age should keep scouts patient with his on-ball development.

21. Toronto Raptors (via Thunder): Miles Sadler (West Virginia)

Position: PG | Size: 6'0", 170 lbs | Age: 19 | Canada

The annual small-guard conversation will come up first with Miles Sadler. Though 6'0", his early production has been very persuasive, thanks to how much control he has creating advantages and capitalizing on them as a finisher and playmaker.

He's using extreme open-floor speed and handling/quickness in half-court creation for generating quality scoring opportunities. Sadler will definitely need to convince scouts his three-point shooting can improve, but the eye test on his jumper doesn't set off any alarms.

22. Detroit Pistons: Brandon McCoy Jr. (Michigan)

Position: PG/SG | Size: 6'5", 190 lbs | Age: 18

A torn ACL will cost Brandon McCoy Jr. his entire freshman season. That will create a difficult decision in May and June, because there's sure to be NBA interest in him, even if he never plays or works out.

Scouts have had years to evaluate McCoy, a disruptive defender, offensive playmaker and improving shooter. Missing the year may cap his stock, but he could still look like an attractive buy-low candidate in the first round.

23. Phoenix Suns (via Timberwolves): Hugo Yimga-Moukouri (Nanterre 92)

Position: SF | Size: 6'8" | Age: 18 | France

Not turning 19 until after the draft, Hugo Yimga-Moukouri is producing in France's LNB Pro A for the second season. He's being used much like last year, as a spot-up scorer who poses a threat with his three-point stroke, slashing and finishing tools.

He'll draw scouts to Nanterre's games regularly with the combination of 6'8" size and shotmaking that screams three-and-D potential. Age will buy him time with scouts who'll want to see more on-ball creation or passing.

24. Memphis Grizzlies: Cheickh Niang (Trento)

Position: SG | Size: 6'5" | Age: 18 | Italy

Cheickh Niang has stood out early by producing efficiently off his explosiveness, shiftiness and improving shotmaking.

Though still reliant on speed and bounce, he's flashed real promise creating with his handle, which his quickness makes even more dangerous.

Niang remains raw at 18 years old, but his skill level is starting to show signs of catching up to his athleticism.

25. Portland Trail Blazers: Caleb Gaskins (Miami)

Position: SF/PF | Size: 6'8", 219 lbs | Age: 18

Caleb Gaskins should generate NBA interest with the ability to stretch the floor as a 4, operate as a 6'8" face-up wing and defend both forward positions.

The eye test should detect an NBA prospect based on Gaskins' physical tools, shooting stroke and overall flashes of inside-out scoring versatility.

26. Philadelphia 76ers: Jason Crowe Jr. (Missouri)

Position: SG | Size: 6'4", 190 lbs | Age: 18

Conversation around Jason Crowe Jr. will revolve around the translatability of his scoring and whether there's everyday playmaking potential to unlock.

The ability to create shots, make tough ones, shoot with range and take over games gives Crowe a microwave mode. Shotmaking, separation tactics and touch distinguish him from the class' other scoring guards.

The question for NBA teams is how well he can execute his shot diet at 6'4", 190 pounds—or if he can switch to a point guard role and organize team offense.

27. Brooklyn Nets (via Rockets): David Mirkovic (Illinois)

Position: PF | Size: 6'9", 250 lbs | Age: 20 | Montenegro

David Mirkovic's versatility is an obvious draw for NBA teams. At 6'9", 250 pounds, he was an effective ball-screen playmaker last season with a handle and passing skill.

He made 57 threes and shot 39.6 percent on pick-and-pops, showing touch elsewhere on floaters/hooks (48.0 percent) and free throws (75.7 percent). And he brought down 8.0 rebounds per game using a strong frame and instincts.

Still, just two dunk attempts and low defensive playmaking rates highlight worrisome athletic limitations. And offseason foot surgery creates uncertainty about his readiness.

28. Boston Celtics: Jordan Scott (Michigan State)

Position: SF | Size: 6'8", 200 lbs | Age: 19

Jordan Scott made a needle-moving impression against Duke, almost all with his defensive tools and instincts. At 6'8", 200 pounds with the way he's able to contest shots and make plays on the ball, capable shooting should be enough for him to draw NBA three-and-D projections.

29. Memphis Grizzlies (via Lakers): Stefan Vaaks (Illinois)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'7", 215 lbs | Age: 21 | Estonia

After checking a coveted mix of boxes last year with 6'7" size, 91 threes and 3.2 assists per game, Stefan Vaaks should open the year on watch lists at Illinois.

Even with glaring athletic issues that limit his rim pressure and defense, Vaaks' shotmaking and passing fit an NBA connector role.

30. Oklahoma City Thunder (via Spurs): Tounde Yessoufou (St. John's)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'5", 220 lbs | Age: 20 | Benin

NBA teams will love Tounde Yessoufou's physical tools, athleticism and motor for transition offense, finishing and defense. Because he totaled more turnovers than assists, there will be extra pressure on his three-point consistency.

At St. John's, with a stacked roster and a seasoned playmaker in Quinn Ellis, Yessoufou is in a favorable spot to get more high-percentage looks off the ball.

31. Utah Jazz (via Nuggets): Dash Daniels (SE Melbourne)

Position: PG/SG | Size: 6'5" | Age: 18 | Australia

Dash Daniels has looked far more confident and decisive this year. Through 11 games, he already has more threes and floaters than he made all of last season.

His shooting and touch are at a different level, important for a guard who lacks the handle and athleticism to blow by defenders or explode around the rim.

Daniels still looks more like a combo 2-guard than a lead playmaker. But if the improved shooting proves legitimate, he'll look like a versatile, attractive guard prospect who can score in ball-screen situations, play off the ball and defend both backcourt positions.

32. Utah Jazz (via Magic): Billy Richmond III (Arkansas)

Position: SF | Size: 6'7", 205 lbs | Age: 20

Billy Richmond III continues to make plays with his athleticism, defense, motor and passing.

Drawing serious NBA interest will mean hitting more threes—or convincing scouts that he can be a non-shooting outlier who adds enough value as a transition scorer, connective piece and defensive disruptor.

33. Philadelphia 76ers (via Warriors): Malachi Moreno (Kentucky)

Position: C | Size: 7'0", 250 lbs | Age: 20

A potential late first-rounder last June, Malachi Moreno returned to be Kentucky's defensive anchor and a more frequently used post player and playmaking hub.

He's looked more threatening this year in the post with his footwork and touch. Still, NBA teams will target Moreno for his rim protection and ability to set up his guards and wings for easier looks offensively.

34. Washington Wizards (via Mavericks): Luigi Suigo (Villanova)

Position: C | Size: 7'3", 289 lbs | Age: 19 | Italy

NBA teams were giving Luigi Suigo first-round looks a few months ago, particularly after he measured nearly 7'3" barefoot with a 9'6" reach.

He should be a focal point this year at Villanova with his combination of overwhelming size around the rim and developing skill. Last year with Mega, he registered a wild 15.0 offensive rebounding percentage and even flashed some shooting range with 18 made threes.

How well he defends ball screens and opponents in space will be key to Suigo's draft stock, although he should remain a regular in the first-round discussion regardless.

35. Toronto Raptors: Amare Bynum (Ohio State)

Position: PF | Size: 6'8", 245 lbs | Age: 19

Amare Bynum should open the season on breakout watch lists after flashing athletic finishing and three-point shooting.

He'll enter the draft discussion if he becomes more consistent from deep and a bigger threat to make plays off the bounce.

36. Washington Wizards (via Pacers): Sam Lewis (Virginia)

Position: SF | Size: 6'7", 210 lbs | Age: 22

Sam Lewis graded as one of last year's most efficient spot-up players. He's breaking out this year with more usage, capitalizing as a transition attacker, ball-screen driver and rhythm shooter.

Though not overly explosive or creative, Lewis has the pro frame, shotmaking and slashing ability for a complementary NBA role.

37. Washington Wizards (via Suns): Matas Vokietaitis (Texas)

Position: C | Size: 7'0", 255 lbs | Age: 19 | Lithuania

Matas Vokietaitis has been highly productive early, using his size and strength for finishing, low-post scoring and offensive rebounding.

He carves out space effectively in the paint, and though he hasn't shown it yet this season, Vokietaitis does look comfortable putting the ball down when there is space to drive.

While there aren't many paths to upside for the 7-footer who isn't known for shot-blocking, NBA teams should see a low-cost, interior presence who'll do work around the basket.

38. Utah Jazz (via Clippers): Kayden Mingo (Baylor)

Position: PG | Size: 6'1", 195 lbs | Age: 19

Kayden Mingo may become a new watch-list priority after he combined for 55 points against Florida and Illinois during preseason.

Though it's not a great time to be a small guard in the NBA draft discussion, he does compensate with a 195-pound frame and excellent floater touch.

Baylor's offense will run through his creativity, which is fueled by downhill driving, shiftiness and improvisation. A 27.2 assist percentage and 3.8 steal percentage highlight two-way playmaking to complement the scoring, though Mingo will still need a significant jump as a shooter to become a coveted 2027 prospect.

39. Sacramento Kings (via Hornets): Trey McKenney (Michigan)

Position: SG | Size: 6'4", 225 lbs | Age: 20

With Michigan losing three lottery picks, Trey McKenney has the freedom to emerge as the team's No. 1 option.

He's looked like a natural scorer since high school, combining a strong 225-pound frame with perimeter creation and shotmaking ability. His 39.1 percent shooting from three and 89.5 percent mark at the free-throw line underscore that scoring touch.

Few signs of playmaking at either end (0.9 assists, 0.4 steals per game) suggest McKenney may be more of a specialist at the NBA level. But his positional strength and shooting indicators should be enough to draw interest.

40. Charlotte Hornets (via Pelicans): Paulius Murauskas (Arizona State)

Position: PF | Size: 6'8", 235 lbs | Age: 22 | Lithuania

Paulius Murauskas put up 18.4 points per game last year, scoring with a balanced mix of post-ups, self-creation and off-ball play as a shotmaker and cutter. He's scoring at an even higher level this year with Arizona State in a featured role. At 6'8", Murauskas' offensive repertoire keeps expanding, and his touch on floaters and free throws suggests he can keep improving as a shooter.

41. New York Knicks (via Wizards): Pryce Sandfort (Nebraska)

Position: SF | Size: 6'7", 215 lbs | Age: 22

Pryce Sandfort's shooting profile was elite last year, highlighted by a 45.0 percent mark on 80 movement threes off screens. He's looked just as potent this season while even showcasing more off-the-dribble scoring in ball-screens situations.

At 6'7", 215 pounds, scouts should start to picture translatable offense tied to his accurate, diverse shotmaking and overall scoring IQ/instincts.

42. Oklahoma City Thunder (via Bulls): Alvaro Folgueiras (Louisville)

Position: PF | Size: 6'10", 230 lbs | Age: 21

More consistency from Alvaro Folgueiras should highlight the versatility scouts are drawn to. At 6'10", he made 36 threes last season, shot 71.4 percent at the rim and registered a 20.7 assist percentage.

The combination of finishing, shooting and passing for a power forward should draw scouts, particularly if Louisville emerges as a top-10 team.

43. Milwaukee Bucks (via Nets): Milan Momcilovic (Kentucky)

Position: SF | Size: 6'9", 220 lbs | Age: 22

Coming off one of the top three-point shooting seasons in history in terms of accuracy (48.7 percent) and volume (7.5 attempts per game), Milan Momcilovic will again audition for an NBA specialist role.

At 6'9", he shot over 45.0 percent on all three major types of threes: stationary catch-and-shoot threes, pull-up threes and movement threes off screens.

He'll be drafted by a team that values a low-cost sure thing over upside or versatility.

44. Sacramento Kings: Rueben Chinyelu (Florida)

Position: C | Size: 6'10", 265 lbs | Age: 23

Rueben Chinyelu learned to use every inch of his size and length, finishing last year as the Naismith Defensive Player of the Year and the nation's second-leading offensive rebounder.

He also improved his post game and free-throw shooting.

While Chinyelu's offensive limitations are well-documented, his tools, production and impact point to a plug-and-play finisher and shot-blocking presence.

45. Milwaukee Bucks: Alex Condon (Florida)

Position: C | Size: 6'11", 236 lbs | Age: 22

Alex Condon has been on NBA radars for two years thanks to his athletic play-finishing, passing and skill flashes.

Even without a jumper, Condon should draw second-round interest from teams that value a big who racked up 48 dunks and averaged 3.6 assists. He just becomes far more interesting with a three-point shot, something he's only teased.

46. Indiana Pacers: Mason Falslev (Utah State)

Position: PG/SG | Size: 6'4", 200 lbs | Age: 25

Mason Falslev has been one of the nation's most productive players through two weeks. He's also one of the oldest, but the level of creativity and craft behind his scoring and playmaking has become too sharp and effective to ignore.

At 6'4", 200 pounds, Falslev should possess enough size, shotmaking firepower and playmaking IQ to fit in at the NBA level, even if the creation doesn't translate as well.

47. Chicago Bulls (via Cavaliers): Jeremy Fears Jr. (Michigan State)

Position: PG | Size: 6'2", 190 lbs | Age: 21

National Player of the Year feels within reach for Jeremy Fears Jr. after he averaged 15.2 points and registered the third-highest assist percentage of the KenPom era.

Beyond his special playmaking feel, he shot 42.0 percent on pull-up jumpers, up from 26.4 percent the year before.

Still, for a 6'2" guard and limited athlete who struggles to generate rim pressure and finish, NBA teams will need to see a bigger jump with his three-point shooting.

48. New Orleans Pelicans (via Heat): Bastien Grasshoff (Le Mans)

A productive start should shift eyes toward Bastien Grasshoff, a 6'6" guard/wing who's clever in pick-and-rolls and threatening around the perimeter. His positional size, craftiness and shotmaking flashes create appealing versatility, though concerns about his athleticism and defensive outlook will put extra pressure on Grasshoff's three-point shooting.

49. New York Knicks: Kellen Thames (Saint Louis)

Position: SF | Size: 6'6", 210 lbs | Age: 23

Though Kellen Thames never averaged 20 minutes or 10 points in any of his four seasons at Saint Louis, an outstanding physical and analytical profile could help him earn NBA looks.

Of the players last year with an offensive box plus-minus over 5.0 and a defensive box plus-minus over 4.0, one was Thames, one was Tyler Tanner and 12 were 2026 first-rounders.

Improved shooting would help, but NBA teams can already picture an outlier who'll impact games with rim pressure, passing and defense.

50. Atlanta Hawks: Silas Demary Jr. (Connecticut)

Position: PG | Size: 6'4", 191 lbs | Age: 22

Silas Demary Jr. has made a name for himself as a floor general with his good decision-making and toughness attacking the rim. He's looked more confident offensively this year, even if his jump shot hasn't fallen consistently yet.

Regardless, there is enough evidence of capable shooting from Demary, and NBA teams will ultimately value his ability to run offense and make the game easier for teammates.

51. New York Knicks (via Thunder): Collin Chandler (BYU)

Position: SG | Size: 6'6", 205 lbs | Age: 22

Now at BYU, Collin Chandler should get a higher-usage role that showcases his athleticism and shotmaking and gives him more ball-screen reps.

He's unlikely to sell teams on his creation, but Chandler is potent in the open floor and behind the arc, a combination that could make him a bench-spark prospect.

52. Detroit Pistons: Amani Hansberry (Virginia Tech)

Position: PF | Size: 6'8", 240 lbs | Age: 22

Scouts could start to picture Amani Hansberry's game translating now that he's a legitimate shooting threat, a plus passer and a solid interior finisher and rebounder.

53. Charlotte Hornets (via Grizzlies): Nolan Winter (Wisconsin)

Position: C | Size: 7'0", 235 lbs | Age: 20

NBA teams should picture a fit for Nolan Winter, who's 7'0" and shot 71.0 percent on rolls and 41.0 percent on pick-and-pops. He's hit over 30 threes in consecutive seasons and shown enough fluidity off the dribble to attack closeouts and fake handoffs.

Winter won't offer overwhelming rim protection, and he tends to fade or go quiet. But he clearly has the size and skill set for a stretch 4/5 and screen-and-score big.

54. Portland Trail Blazers (via Timberwolves): Marc-Owen Fozdo Dada (ASVEL)

Marc-Owen Fozdo Dada is entering the draft conversation with tough baskets and defense in the LNB Pro A and EuroLeague.

Quick and physical, he's at his best getting downhill, putting pressure on the rim or creating playmaking chances.

His shooting needs work, but it's functional, and he impacts games elsewhere with breakdown ability and defensive activity.

55. Portland Trail Blazers: Andrej Stojakovic (Illinois)

Position: SF | Size: 6'7", 205 lbs | Age: 22 | Greece/Serbia

Andrej Stojakovic needs to show improved shooting, but he was far more efficient inside the arc last year. He has NBA wing size, scoring instincts and some impressive self-creation skill. A more reliable three-point shot would unlock three-level scoring and make Stojakovic a more believable NBA prospect.

56. San Antonio Spurs (via Rockets): John Blackwell (Duke)

Position: SG | Size: 6'5", 205 lbs | Age: 21

After averaging 19.1 points at Wisconsin, John Blackwell is now a good candidate to become the top scorer for a national title contender.

He's an easy fit with his balanced mix of creation and off-ball shotmaking. His limited athleticism around the rim and modest playmaking will likely keep his NBA buzz from matching his college impact.

57. Philadelphia 76ers: Miles Byrd (Providence)

Position: SG/SF | Size: 6'6", 200 lbs | Age: 22

Miles Byrd's incredible defensive instincts have returned, as evidenced by his 21 steals through four games. He hasn't made a major jump as a scorer, but Byrd's shotmaking has been persuasive enough for teams to gamble on three-and-D potential in the second round.

58. Phoenix Suns (via Celtics): Finley Bizjack (West Virginia)

Position: SG | Size: 6'4", 190 lbs | Age: 21

With Miles Sadler and Finley Bizjack in the backcourt, scouts should be regulars at West Virginia games. Bizjack's potential NBA appeal stems from his shotmaking versatility, scoring instincts and ability to generate offense from on and off the ball. His touch, footwork and confidence give him a chance to carve out a role as a perimeter scoring specialist, though questions remain about whether he can consistently separate and finish against NBA size and athleticism.

59. Miami Heat (via Spurs): Somto Cyril (Miami)

Position: C | Size: 6'11", 260 lbs | Age: 21

Powerful at 260 pounds with a 7'7" wingspan and athletic leaping ability, Somto Cyril led the nation in dunks while registering a 10.6 block percentage. NBA teams should see a two-way weapon around the basket. But his turnover percentage was triple his assist percentage, and a career 54.1 free-throw percentage could make it hard to give him starter's minutes.

60. Brooklyn Nets (via 76ers): Money Williams (Boston College)

Position: PG | Size: 6'4", 206 lbs | Age: 21

After averaging 20.6 points and 4.7 assists for Montana, Money Williams will have a chance to validate that production in the ACC. Limited athleticism and shooting range, plus 4.1 turnovers per game, kept draft buzz from building last year. Scouts could take Williams seriously if his creation and scoring craft translate against tougher competition.

articles.title: Biggest NBA Surprises and Disappointments After 1 Month
articles.summary: It's still early in the 2026-27 NBA season, but surprises and disappointments have already emerged.
articles.body:
It's still early in the 2026-27 NBA season, but surprises and disappointments have already emerged.

The surprises have been players returning from season-ending injuries, a young upstart, a rookie making waves, and some late offseason signings stepping up—all of which are changing the course of their teams' futures.

The disappointments include injuries, unfortunately, as well as the champs' slow start, a young team not living up to expectations, and a fun story last season turning sour this season.

It is a long season, and these early-season signs may just be a small-sample effect. Some of them, however, might signal what's coming this season for some of these teams.

Houston, you are a problem for the rest of the league.

It is early in the season, but it's easy to tell how different this year's Houston Rockets are compared to last season. Last season felt cursed from the start with Fred VanVleet's torn ACL. The season went downhill after the All-Star break, and the Lakers knocked Houston out of the playoffs.

For starters, Fred VanVleet's return has brought order to everyone's role. Amen Thompson does not have to be a primary playmaker but can now work as an off-ball cutter and be a pure disruptor. Kevin Durant has someone setting him up as he comes off pin-downs. Alperen Sengun does not have to be the main facilitator of the offense. VanVleet has brought order to the Rockets' offense, which is second in offensive rating .

Also buried in Houston's success is the rise of Jabari Smith Jr.'s play. On opening night, he dropped 30 points and is shooting 38.6 percent from three to start the year. Adding another legit shooter to this roster goes a long way toward spreading the floor.

Besides the offense, the defense has been top-notch. Thompson is a great defender, and off the bench, Ime Udoka can unleash Tari Eason and Marcus Smart. Houston looks like a contender right out of the gate. Something that seemed so far away after last season's playoffs.

Even with a relatively soft schedule, no one could have anticipated the Memphis Grizzlies starting the season 9-4. Especially coming off a 25-win campaing last year.

Of course, adding the third pick in the draft to the roster helps, especially when the player is as NBA-ready as Cameron Boozer.

Boozer has been electric. His feel for the game is so smooth. He is nearly averaging a double-double, and he's doing it while shooting just 39.3 percent from the field. His passing has really impressed, with 5.4 assists per game. His timing and floor reading have already proven to be at a high level.

Second-year Cedric Coward is shooting a whopping 43.9 percent from three and is grabbing 8.8 boards. Ty Jerome is raining floaters consistently in the lane, including a 45-point opening night. To start the season, the Grizzlies are top ten in defensive rating and third in offensive rating; that is rarefied air.

This start to the season, and banking wins so early, should put the Grizzlies in contention for at least a play-in spot.

There was no doubt on draft night that the Golden State Warriors landed Yaxel Lendeborg and made a great pick. A player with a high IQ, a great motor, and good defense was always going to be a great fit. No one was prepared for him to be a monster scorer.

Lendeborg's scoring has been on display all season. He's the Warriors' second-leading scorer, averaging 21.0 points a game on near 50/40 shooting splits, plus 4.1 assists and 7.1 boards. He has already dropped more than 30 points in two games this season. He has been a massive impact player for the Warriors.

Look no further than Lendeborg's breakout performance against the Denver Nuggets. He was a massive disruptor defensively, finishing the game with 31 points, 12 rebounds, and six assists. He is a force on both ends of the floor and is an absolute game changer.

Lendeborg has been a breath of fresh air for the Warriors. They have not had a player of this caliber in a long while. He will be a contender for the Rookie of the Year race.

There is no happier story in the NBA than the return of Damian Lillard to the Portland Trail Blazers. It was a year-long comeback after recovering from the torn Achilles he suffered during the 2024 playoffs. With his return, Dame time is back!

Lillard is coming into a different team than the one he left years ago. Playing off of Deni Avdija (and Ja Morant before his injury) has allowed Lillard more catch-and-shoot opportunities. He's averaging 4.6 a game , the most ever in his career.

Now, all that said, Lillard is not ripping the cord as frequently as most are used to. But that will come over time as the season gets going. More importantly, he's back, and he's playing with other players who can create for him instead of him creating for himself constantly.

That has produced wins as the Blazers are currently 9-4 and kept some miles off of Lillard's legs.

One of the biggest needs for the Lakers late in the offseason was the need for perimeter defense. They picked up two guys—Ziarie Williams and Matisse Thybulle—on relatively low-cost contracts, and early in the season, that has paid off.

Williams, in his sixth year, has never been more than just a defensive role player. Prior to this season, his best three-point percentage was 34.3 percent, and that was last season. This year, it has jumped more than 10 percentage points to 45.5 percent. This is a huge revelation because it lets the Lakers play him on the floor for his defense, and his shooting provides spacing for the offense.

Over the last few seasons in Portland, Thybulle has improved as a three-point shooter but has played only a limited number of games over four years. He has always been a defensive specialist with limited range. That is no longer the case, as this season he's shooting 39.3 percent on 4.3 attempts per game.

Before these offseason signings, the Lakers had a major hole in their perimeter defense. They were short on point-of-attack defenders. Not only have these two wings provided, but they have also been hitting enough shots to keep defenses honest. Getting this level of production from these players has been a surprise, so surprising that JJ Redick has decided to insert both of them into the starting lineup.

Injuries are always disappointing. This is not NBA2K. The feature cannot be turned off. But the rash of injuries right now has marred the start of the season.

Everyone has been affected. Below are two major examples, but the list of injured players would fill the entire column.

The first few games of Anthony Edwards' season had many speculating that he could vault himself into MVP contention. Then it was announced that he had his knee scoped and would be out for the next two months. That ends that MVP campaign.

The Oklahoma City Thunder were one of the favorites to win the championship this season, then the injuries hit. Jalen Williams suffered a gruesome injury, and Cason Wallace tore his labrum in the same game. Then it was announced that Chet Holmgren will be out for the next eight to 10 weeks, recovering from a partial patellar tendon tear.

Unfortunately, injuries are a factor every season. Teams have to be ready for them.

To start this season, though, it has been massively disappointing to see so many injuries to so many crucial players.

This was supposed to be the season the Utah Jazz climbed out of the tanking basement and into competitive basketball. The thought was that with Jaren Jackson Jr., Laurie Markkanen, Keyonte George, Darryn Petersen, and Ace Bailey, the Jazz would field a competitive bunch. They may not have been a top-six playoff team, but at the very least, they could be a play-in contender.

That is not how anything has played out. It is easy to point to the injuries (see: previous slide) like losing Jusuf Nurkić, but that does not entirely explain the no-show on opening night. A 20-point loss in Memphis was not the start they hoped for in this era of trying to compete after a few seasons of tanking.

This was all before Utah lost JJJ to an MCL tear and Markkanen to a wrist injury.

A few bright spots have emerged this season, though. Bailey has leveled up as a defender, and George has been sensational, averaging 21.3 points and 6.2 assists. Petersen has come on strong as of late, averaging 23.2 points.

Despite all that, being 1-13 to start the season is a disappointment for a team that was expected to compete for a play-in spot

It has been an uneven start for the New York Knicks. So it's worth asking if the championship hangover is real.

The 7-6 Knicks are off to a slow start. At the start of the season, they simply were not making shots. Jalen Brunson has rebounded from an awful shooting start to get back to 38.3 percent from three, but both Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges are shooting below 30 percent.

More troubling than the shooting woes, the Knicks have just not been a good clutch team to start the year. They are 2-6 this year in close games after going 21-13 last season.

The Knicks started the season 0-3. The first defending champs to start like this was the 2011-12 Dallas Mavericks, who finished the season 36-30 during a shortened season. New York has faced tough opponents but is already 0-2 against the Philadelphia 76ers and 0-1 against the Boston Celtics.

This is still very early in the season, and it's safe to assume Brunson and company will find their flow as the season goes on. The schedule does indeed get easier. That is the beauty of an 82-game season; it will be forgiving for an early slow start with the talent the Knicks have.

The Phoenix Suns were the "feel good" story last season. They were praised for the change in their culture with credit going to then-first-year head coach Jordan Ott and newly acquired Dillon Brooks.

The result was a first-round exit, and this season has started as the exact opposite of a feel-good story.

Opening night was a bad sign for Phoenix. They got blasted by 41 points by the Portland Trail Blazers. It took a 43-point night from Devin Booker and the Golden State Warriors resting Stephen Curry for the Suns to get their first win of the season.

The vibes that were once lauded now seem completely off in Phoenix. One pain point is starting Jalen Green over Collin Gillespie at point guard. The team needs a table-setting point guard, and there are already rumblings of making a move.

The roster issue goes beyond just a point guard. Mark Williams has been out since the beginning of the season, and second-year big man Khaman Maluach still seems far from being a true contributor.

If things continue on this path, the Suns might need to consider tweaking the roster.

*All stats are current entering games on Monday, Nov. 16.

Mo Dakhil spent six years with the Los Angeles Clippers and two years with the San Antonio Spurs as a video coordinator, as well as three years with the Australian men's national team. Follow him on X, @MoDakhil_NBA .

articles.title: Latest 2027 Men's NCAA Tournament Bracket Projections
articles.summary: The 2026-27 men's college basketball season is only two weeks old, but some of these early games have already had a March feel to them.
articles.body:
The 2026-27 men's college basketball season is only two weeks old, but some of these early games have already had a March feel to them.

Not so much the Champions Classic nightcap between Kansas and Kentucky. But Michigan State-Duke and Illinois-Texas Tech set the stage for a big week of bracketology movement.

We still won't have NET rankings for another couple of weeks—last year's initial rankings were released on Dec. 1—which means "quads" won't be part of the discourse just yet. Even when those rankings arrive, there's little reason to expect them to resemble the final version some 100 days later.

For the diehards, though, bracketology is all about the season-long journey—the constant twists and turns that eventually bring us to the final product. And that journey is well underway.

Remember, results from the first half of November mean just as much to the selection committee as the results from the first half of March. In fact, one could easily argue these early results are even more important , because they establish the baseline for how teams will be judged for the rest of the season.

With that in mind, here is our latest glance into the Selection Sunday crystal ball.

Later in the season, automatic bids will be determined by conference record. For now, they are determined by KenPom ranking.

Also, please forgive any first-round pairings which are rematches of scheduled nonconference games. We won't start worrying about avoiding those until shortly after Feast Week.

Following their losses on Tuesday night, Duke (No. 7 overall) and Illinois (No. 8 overall) slipped slightly out of the conversation for the top seed line. Though, with the Blue Devils hosting the Illini Tuesday night, one of them is going to jump right back into the mix—while the other will be reeling at 3-2.

That game is merely the tip of the iceberg, though, as far as marquee matchups are concerned over the course of the next 72 hours.

As far as already scheduled games go, we've got Michigan State playing at Tennessee (No. 17 overall) on Tuesday and Connecticut playing at Arizona (No. 9 overall) on Wednesday.

If they happen to both lose those road games, get ready for all of the seeding carnage, because we've also got Florida, Houston and Kansas all competing in the Players Era 8 tournament this Tuesday-Thursday.

Most likely, all three will win on Tuesday. The Gators draw Notre Dame, the Cougars get Rutgers and the Jayhawks open with UNLV. But if they do each prevail in the quarters, it'll be Florida vs. Houston on Wednesday with one of them also running into Kansas on Thursday, probably in the championship game.

That means there will be a minimum of four losses suffered by top-nine teams in the next few days. So, if you disagree with this ranking, just wait for the inevitable shakeup.

Unfortunately, though, someone forgot to tell Virginia that all the top title contenders are facing major tests this week. The Cavaliers merely have home games against Old Dominion and Loyola MD. But they've already made quite the early impression by trouncing Arkansas and winning at Maryland. Can't wait to watch them face UConn at Madison Square Garden the week before Christmas.

10 Words on Each of the 10 'Bubbliest' Teams

Fifth-to-Last In : Notre Dame Fighting Irish—Massive opportunity in Players Era 8, facing Florida Tuesday night.

Fourth-to-Last In : Marquette Golden Eagles—Struggled to make anything in losses to Michigan and Missouri.

Third-to-Last In : Cincinnati Bearcats—Slides back into the projected field after blowing out Dayton.

Second-to-Last In : Santa Clara Broncos—Survived against New Mexico behind big night from Elijah Mahi.

Last Team In : Creighton Bluejays—Split with Iowa and Kansas State; narrowly remains in field.

First Team Out : Iowa Hawkeyes—After losing consecutive nail-biters, Iowa is our first team out.

Second Team Out : Kentucky Wildcats—Remove preseason bias and Kentucky isn't a top 100 team .

Third Team Out : Providence Friars—How about Miles Byrd racking up 10 steals against Colorado?

Fourth Team Out : Pittsburgh Panthers—Nice victory at Butler, but beat Villanova and we'll talk.

Fifth Team Out : DePaul Blue Demons—20-point win at Northwestern? Better at least acknowledge undefeated DePaul.

New 2027 NBA Mock Draft with Full 2-Round Predictions, Pro Comps

7 Teams in the Projected Field : 6. Virginia, 7. Duke, 23. Louisville, 24. Miami (FL), 46. Virginia Tech, 47. North Carolina, 50. Notre Dame

Also Considered : Pittsburgh, Florida State, N.C. State, SMU

Biggest Development : Losses Left and Right

Most of the major conferences had one, maybe two of their projected tournament teams take one on the chin this past week.

But outside of Virginia re-asserting itself as one of the early threats to make the Final Four, the ACC left much to be desired.

It started with Duke getting slightly manhandled by Michigan State in the Champions Classic. The final margin was only six points, but at no point did it feel like the Blue Devils were the better team in that one. They did respond with a 43-point drubbing of SIU-Edwardsville, but let's see how Duke looks Tuesday night against an Illinois squad that is also reeling from a recent loss.

Friday was the much bigger blow to this conference as a whole, as both Clemson (vs. Georgetown) and North Carolina (vs. Georgia) lost at home in games they ought to have won. The Tar Heels were out-rebounded, yet again, and shot just 9-for-38 from three-point distance. It might be a long first season for Michael Malone.

And then on Sunday, Louisville turned an early 23-6 lead into a 20-point loss at Memphis. Jayden Reid had another masterful game for the Tigers, but the Cardinals simply had no answer on defense for anything Memphis threw at them after those first few minutes.

Beyond that, St. John's ran away from Syracuse, Stanford lost at UNLV and Florida State was unable to pull a fast one on Florida. None of those three were in our projected field one week ago, but they slip even further out of the conversation now.

10 Teams in the Projected Field : 4. Kansas, 5. Houston, 9. Arizona, 11. Texas Tech, 20. BYU, 21. Iowa State, 31. Baylor, 39. West Virginia, 43. TCU, 53. Cincinnati

Also Considered : Oklahoma State, Arizona State, UCF

Biggest Development : Texas Tech Makes a Statement

In a vivid early reminder that on-campus nonconference games are the best kind of nonconference games, Texas Tech vs. Illinois stole the show on what was supposed to be Champions Classic night.

The Red Raiders stormed out to a 22-point lead in the first half, as the roof repeatedly threatened to blow right off of United Supermarkets Arena.

The Illini eventually trimmed the deficit all the way back down to just one, but never could get over the hump en route to an 84-78 TTU win.

It was Jamichael Stillwell's first game after getting a temporary restraining order for eligibility, and he was huge off the bench for 11 points and 13 rebounds. Fellow transfers Cruz Davis and Dra Gibbs-Lawhorn also led the charge with a combined 35 points.

The real development, however, was that the Red Raiders defeated one of the top threats to win the national championship despite getting virtually nothing out of Darrion Williams. He averaged 13.5 points per game over the previous three seasons, but he missed all five of his field-goal attempts on his way to just four points.

If he eventually snaps out of his slow start and Texas Tech gets J.T. Toppin back from his torn ACL at some point, this team is going to be a terror.

Elsewhere in the Big 12, Kansas (in its first game sans Melvin Council Jr.) destroyed Kentucky by 20 and Arizona picked up a quality road win over Auburn. Even projected Big 12 bottom-feeder Kansas State scored an impressive home win over Creighton.

Had Baylor been able to win that back-and-forth battle with Texas in San Antonio on Sunday, it would've been a darn near perfect week for this league.

7 Teams in the Projected Field : 2. Connecticut, 15. St. John's, 36. Villanova, 44. Xavier, 48. Georgetown, 52. Marquette, 55. Creighton

Biggest Development : Back to Square One with Marquette

Between its opening week games against Mercyhurst and Detroit Mercy, Marquette had those offenses crying "Mercy!" while allowing just 37.5 points per blowout win.

Against actual competition this week, though, the Golden Eagles were the ones struggling to generate offense.

At Michigan, Marquette did force 15 turnovers, but it shot 13-for-38 (34.2 percent) on two-pointers en route to a 14-point loss. Unanimous preseason All-Big East first team guard Nigel James Jr. missed all 11 of his field-goal attempts and committed four turnovers in a disastrous night he may never forget.

In Sunday's game against Missouri (in Chicago), Marquette suffocated the Tigers through the first 32.5 minutes. The HAVOC defense that Shaka Smart patented a lifetime ago with VCU was on full display, forcing 21 turnovers in a 52-41 game. It was all for naught, though, after Missouri closed out the game on an extended 28-12 run, as Marquette shot below 40 percent from the field for a second consecutive game.

Neither was a bad loss, of course. In fact, Marquette was a slight underdog in each. But after ranking 265th in field-goal percentage last year with a mark of 43.8 percent, the Golden Eagles are sitting at 42.8 percent through four games.

Turnover-forcing defense is great, but can Marquette figure out how to do something after it generates those takeaways?

Aside from Marquette, though, it was a respectable week from the Big East.

Creighton lost the aforementioned game at Kansas State, but bounced back with a nice one-point, neutral-site victory over Iowa. And on Friday alone, Connecticut smoked Ohio State while Georgetown (at Clemson), DePaul (at Northwestern) and Xavier (vs. Mississippi State in West Virginia) all picked up pretty convincing wins away from home against power conference competition. Those are the types of nights in November that can pay dividends on Selection Sunday.

10 Teams in the Projected Field : 3. Michigan State, 8. Illinois, 14. UCLA, 16. Nebraska, 22. Michigan, 26. USC, 29. Indiana, 34. Minnesota, 35. Wisconsin, 38. Ohio State

Biggest Development : Michigan State Might Be A Monster

The Spartans were a top 10 team coming into the season, and then they destroyed both Quinnipiac and Toledo in their tune-ups for the Champions Classic.

In other words, they didn't exactly come out of nowhere on Tuesday night.

But they controlled that game against Duke from the outset, scoring on each of their first five possessions while the Blue Devils managed points on just three of their first 16 possessions.

National Player of the Year frontrunner Jeremy Fears Jr. finished with 18 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds, while Jordan Scott set the tone on defense with six blocks and a pair of steals.

Duke managed to make the final score (79-73) look respectable, but this was one of those games where every time you checked the score, you were left wondering how the clearly better team wasn't winning by more.

Michigan State proceeded to drop 106 points on Northern Iowa three nights later, eclipsing the century mark in a regulation game for just the second time in the past six seasons.

The Spartans have another big one coming up Tuesday night at Tennessee, but they'll carry a projected No. 1 seed into that clash.

At the other end of the spectrum, what a gut-wrenching pair of losses Iowa suffered this week.

Ty'Reek Coleman missed what would have been the game-winning free throw with one second left in regulation against Virginia Tech. The Hokies went on to win by five in overtime. And against Creighton, the Hawkeyes rallied from 14 down and had several chances to win in the final minute, but Peyton McCollum's game-winning three-point attempt hit the front of the iron to finalize a one-point loss.

Iowa was a No. 9 seed last week, but just barely missing the field feels almost too on the nose at the moment.

12 Teams in the Projected Field : 2. Florida, 10. Vanderbilt, 12. Texas, 13. Alabama, 17. Tennessee, 18. LSU, 25. Texas A&M, 27. Arkansas, 28. Georgia, 32. Auburn, 33. Missouri, 40. Ole Miss

Biggest Development : Would You Like the Good News or the Bad News?

Let's start with the good news for the SEC and highlight LSU's road win over Gonzaga.

The Zags led by 13 with eight minutes to go and still held a nine-point edge with less than four minutes left in regulation, but the Tigers refused to go away. Abdi Bashir Jr. hit three triples in the final five-plus minutes of the second half to help draw them back to within striking distance. But it was Donovan Dent who delivered the dagger three-pointer with one second remaining—both at the end of the first half and at the end of the second half, by the way.

We weren't sure what to make of LSU's first three wins (each by 40-plus points) over New Orleans, Texas Southern and Louisiana Tech, but wins at Gonzaga don't exactly grow on trees. Question the ethics of the roster construction all you want, but the early results have been mighty impressive. LSU skyrockets from a No. 11 seed all the way to a No. 5 seed.

Also good for the SEC, Vanderbilt destroyed a Memphis team that has otherwise already beaten Iowa State, Louisville and VCU, while Georgia (at North Carolina) and Texas (vs. Baylor in San Antonio) picked up solid wins away from home.

But, hoo boy, Kentucky might be a trainwreck.

Even prior to this past week, that 89-80 home win over James Madison was a close game for way longer than anyone expected. JMU just fired up three-pointer after three-pointer and never let the Wildcats pull away.

However, that was merely the precursor to a 20-point shellacking at the hands of Kansas and an almost-disaster for the ages against Northern Arizona.

In the former, they couldn't slow down Tre White or Tyran Stokes, and they inexplicably couldn't create any good looks for Milan Momcilovic, who played 36 minutes and took just seven shots. Kansas played extremely well in its first game without Melvin Council Jr. (foot), but that game seemed to say more about the Wildcats than it did about the Jayhawks.

And then on Friday night, Kentucky shot 42.3 percent from deep, shot 69.0 percent inside the arc and committed just four turnovers...yet still needed a last-second Alex Wilkins three-pointer to spare them from a loss that would have rivaled Robert Morris, Saint Peter's and Evansville in Big Blue Nation infamy.

If Mark Pope wasn't already on the hottest seat in the country, he certainly is now. We'll put the Wildcats back in our projected field just as soon as they look like they want to be in it.

Mid-Majors Summary (A10, AAC, MVC, MWC, P12, WCC)

9 Teams in the Projected Field : 19. Gonzaga, 30. Memphis, 37. Utah State, 42. Saint Louis, 45. Grand Canyon, 49. VCU, 51. Saint Mary's, 54. Santa Clara, 57. Murray State

Biggest Development : Utah State Scores Big; Santa Clara Enters the Fray

It was hardly a banner week for this tier of two-bid or three-bid hopeful leagues. In addition to Gonzaga getting clipped at home by LSU, Memphis (at Vanderbilt), Boise State (Nebraska) and Saint Louis (vs. High Point) each suffered a loss by double digits. [Though, Memphis more than made up for its L by pummeling Louisville.]

Worst of all, Nevada suffered not one, but two losses, soundly defeated at UC Santa Barbara before a close home loss to Utah Valley. The Wolf Pack was our fourth team out one week ago, but they are completely off the radar at this point.

Two teams did make quite the positive impression, though, in Utah State and Santa Clara.

For the former, it was the relentlessness of an offense doing its best "Hank Gathers era Loyola Marymount" impression, putting up 118 vs. Utah Tech and 120 vs. UC San Diego in consecutive games. In the latter—against a respectable mid-major, we might add—the Aggies eclipsed 90 points in less than 25 minutes. Across the two routs, they shot a combined 35-for-71 from three-point range. They'll still face BYU, USC, New Mexico and SMU before Pac-12 play begins, but those USU-Gonzaga matchups promise to be thrilling.

Meanwhile, Santa Clara won at North Texas before winning a home game against New Mexico. Neither currently looks likely to end up as a Quad 1 result, but that's a solid one-two punch for a team that spent seemingly the entire 2025-26 campaign on the bubble.

The Broncos are now 5-0 and get a home game against VCU on Thursday in yet another opportunity to make a good early impression.

21 Teams in the Projected Field : 41. High Point, 56. UC Santa Barbara, 58. Wright State, 59. UNC Wilmington, 60. Akron, 61. McNeese, 62. Montana State, 63. Western Kentucky, 64. Furman, 65. South Dakota State, 66. Penn, 67. Central Arkansas, 68. Old Dominion, 69. Howard, 70. Vermont, 71. Lipscomb, 72. American, 73. Bethune-Cookman, 74. Iona, 75. Tennessee State, 76. Long Island

Biggest Development : High Point Hits a High Point

High Point had already been one of the better mid-majors over the past two seasons, securing a No. 13 seed in 2025 and a No. 12 seed (including a first-round victory over Wisconsin) last year. In both seasons, the Panthers finished just outside the top 80 on KenPom.

Could it be that they were just getting warmed up?

On Sunday, High Point improved to 5-0 with a 10-point road win over a Saint Louis team that certainly would've been ranked in the AP poll right now if it had protected home court.

Even more impressive, High Point did so without Cam'Ron Fletcher, its seventh-year senior who is averaging 12.8 points and 8.0 rebounds, but did not travel for this game due to an illness.

In his stead, the Panthers clamped down on defense, allowing just 58 points to a team that had averaged 102.3 PPG in its first three contests. They racked up 17 steals, keeping the Billikens from getting into any sort of offensive rhythm until it was too little, too late.

High Point is now hovering just outside the top 50 on KenPom, very much in "at-large bid, if necessary" territory. And aside from a road game against LSU on Dec. 18, KenPom gives the Panthers at least an 81 percent win probability in each game left on its schedule—as well as a 4.5 percent chance of an undefeated regular season.

We'll see if they can at least make it through the next month with a zero in the loss column, but it sure looks as though we'll be spending a lot of time talking about High Point over the course of the next few months.

articles.title: Indiana Fever Makes Big Caitlin Clark Statement After Jeopardy! Features Her Yet Again
articles.summary: The Caitlin Clark effect hit Jeopardy! and the internet erupted overnight.
articles.body:
From SNL to Jeopardy! , Caitlin Clark's pop-culture takeover reaches a new milestone. The Indiana Fever star guard got another shoutout on Jeopardy!, and fans are losing their minds over it.

Clark has already crossed into mainstream pop culture through SNL , Nike , and Taylor Swift adjacency, and the Jeopardy! clue is the latest proof. It also frames her as a full-blown cultural phenomenon rather than just a sports star.

The television show Jeopardy! featured Clark with a clue centered on the "Caitlin Clark effect." The clue highlighted her widespread impact on basketball viewership and culture during the WNBA offseason.

The Fever guard was the answer to a clue in the "women in sports" category that read: "THE INDIANA FEVER'S NO.1 DRAFT PICK IN 2024, SHE'S HAD A GREAT "EFFECT" ON WOMEN'S BASKETBALL."

Without missing a beat, a contestant named Roger answered for $400, "It was Clark!"

The Caitlin Clark effect refers to the increase in popularity of women's basketball attributed to the Fever guard.

The Fever shared this moment on their official X (formerly Twitter) account, and the post has since gone viral.

One fan commented under the post, "Even Jeopardy knows who's selling the tickets 😂."

Resharing the clip, another fan wrote, "Caitlin Clark has become so mainstream that her impact on women's basketball was featured as a clue on Jeopardy."

Meanwhile, another fan called Clark, "THE FACE OF WOMEN'S SPORTS!! 💯."

Tagging Clark, another fan wrote, "you know you've made it when you get on jeopardy @CaitlinClark22."

One fan shared similar sentiments, as they commented, "That's when you know you have officially hit the ICON status. When you have become a jeopardy question. Congrats 👏 👏."

"Jeopardy love them some Caitlin Clark answers. This is the fourth time," joked another fan.

This was indeed not the first time Clark had been mentioned on the NBC show. She and Simone Biles were among the clues in an episode from last year, which featured Game Two of the 2025 Jeopardy! Invitational Tournament finals.

During April 2024's Jeopardy! Invitational Tournament , she was the $400 answer in the sports category to the clue : "In 2024 this Iowa athlete sunk one of her trademark logo 3-pointers & set the all-time NCAA women's scoring record."

One of the all-time great Jeopardy champions, Amy Schneider, had the correct answer on April 5, 2024. Later that same night, Clark faced Paige Bueckers in the NCAA Women's Final Four and helped lead the Iowa Hawkeyes past the UConn Huskies, 71-69.

Clark scored 21 points to help the Hawkeyes secure that thrilling win, advancing Iowa to the National Championship game for the second consecutive year. The 2024 National Championship game was the first NCAA women's basketball title game to outdraw the men's title game.

A few days later, the Fever selected Clark with the first overall pick in the 2024 WNBA Draft. Reporting on Indiana's revenue and online following in 2024, Forbes said they are "becoming the most followed women's basketball team online."

USA Today columnist Christine Brennan even argued that Clark's popularity stemmed from her style of play rather than media promotion, noting it "grew organically from the heartland to the coasts."

Clark's Fever jersey sold out in less than an hour on the day of the 2024 WNBA Draft. Her jersey was the best-selling in the WNBA and second in all North American basketball after Stephen Curry.

Speaking to The Indianapolis Star about his finding that Clark was responsible for more than 25 percent of the WNBA's revenue in the 2024 season, Indiana University Columbus finance professor Ryan Brewer said, "The numbers are so staggering. They don't even seem real."

Brewer also told NBC News that Clark's presence had increased the overall value of the league to a minimum of $875 million, with potential over one billion dollars.

Currently, Clark is continuing to expand her mainstream crossover beyond basketball following her third season in the league with the Fever. She recently made an appearance on The Tonight Show and talked about her debut children's book , which days later reached number one on The New York Times Best Sellers list.

As Clark continues her offseason schedule, her Jeopardy recognition underscores the sustained profile she brings entering the 2027 WNBA season.

articles.title: Celtics’ Jayson Tatum Makes Feelings Clear on Steve Kerr’s Olympic Benching
articles.summary: The Boston Celtics are 11-3 and Jayson Tatum has been at the center of everything they have built this season. He is producing at an elite level while still...
articles.body:
The Boston Celtics are 11-3 and Jayson Tatum has been at the center of everything they have built this season. He is producing at an elite level while still working his way back from an Achilles rupture. The leadership, the scoring, the standard he is setting for the group around him have defined the early months.

In a new interview with Boardroom's "Cover Story" feature, Tatum revisited his experience at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Team USA won gold, but JT's role was far smaller than expected coming off the most successful stretch of his career.

Tatum opened up about how he first realized things were not going to go the way he expected.

Before the team boarded the bus for the first game against Serbia, head coach Steve Kerr pulled the Celtics star aside.

"Steve was like, 'Kevin is back, so we're going to have to try to figure something out with the lineup,'" Tatum said . "He was like, 'Just be patient.' What the f— did that mean? Why are you telling me that?"

The picture filled in once the game started.

"Once I didn't get in in the first quarter, I was like, 'Oh, some fishy s—t going on,'" Tatum said. "That's when it kind of hit me like, 'Oh, that's what he was trying to tell me without trying to tell me.'"

Tatum did not play in either game against Serbia. He suited up for only four of six contests, logging fewer minutes than every teammate except Tyrese Haliburton.

The timing added another layer. Weeks earlier, Tatum had won a championship. He was All-NBA First Team. He was on the cover of NBA 2K. JT arrived in Paris riding the best stretch of his career.

"I just won the Finals…I was All-NBA first team. I was on the cover of 2K…I was having a crazy summer," Tatum said. "Then, to get to the Olympics and that happened. It was hard to process."

Through it all, the Celtics star kept the focus on the team. He stayed ready, stayed engaged, and helped bring home the gold medal.

"I just tried my best to not make it about me," Tatum said. "Still be the best teammate I could."

The Olympics gave Tatum a different kind of experience than he anticipated. He responded by handling it with professionalism and competing when called upon. The gold medal still went around his neck.

Everything since, from the Achilles comeback to the way he has led this team through the first months of the season, reflects a player who took what happened in Paris and used it as motivation.

Tatum is playing with an edge this year. Now everyone knows a little more about where part of that comes from.

articles.title: Jaylen Brown injury update: Philadelphia 76ers star gets concerning news after getting into No. 1 seed in the East
articles.summary: Jaylen Brown left Monday’s win in Brooklyn with 1:44 to play, and the Philadelphia 76ers are now waiting on word about a cut head and a tight left
articles.body: Jaylen Brown left Monday’s win in Brooklyn with 1:44 to play, and the Philadelphia 76ers are now waiting on word about a cut head and a tight left hamstring. The Sixers beat the Nets 135-123 for their third straight win and took back the No. 1 seed in the East. Brown finished with 31 points and 13 rebounds, but a head collision with Julius Randle in the fourth quarter left a bloody cut on the left forehead. Brown came back, then returned to the bench with hamstring tightness. Coach Nick Nurse used that exact word. More checks are set for Tuesday.What is Jaylen Brown’s injury status after the Nets game?Brown said both areas were checked after the win. The head looks fine. The hamstring needs watching. “My head is OK, and the hamstring, it’s a little tight,” the five-time All-Star said. He could not pin down when the leg started to act up, only that it happened during the game. Nurse said the exit came from tightness in the left hamstring, not the head injury.The plan for now is simple. Brown will “take a look at it tomorrow” and “see how it feels and go from there.” An MRI is possible, and no results were in yet.Brown had the option to sit after the head blow. He chose to come back with a bandage over the cut. The Sixers led by seven when Brown checked himself out, and Brooklyn cut it to four before Philadelphia closed it out. “I wanted to make sure we got the win,” Brown said. He added, “It would have been a lot worse of an injury if we had lost.”Brown’s second straight 31-point night and the Magic gameBrown shot 9-for-19 from the floor and 10-for-13 at the line on Monday. He added 13 rebounds and four assists, and matched the 31 points he scored in the game before. The 2024 NBA Finals MVP is still settling in with a new team, and he said so plainly. “Still got a long way to go,” Brown said, “but just starting to feel a little bit more at home.” He also said he is more comfortable with “the guys and the group and my spots,” which shows in the numbers.Brooklyn made it interesting. The Nets outscored Philadelphia 64-58 in the second half, yet the Sixers held on to move to 12-3.Wednesday brings the Orlando Magic, and Brown’s availability is uncertain. LeBron James sat out Monday with a back injury and is expected to return.
